steps.stepGoal: Students will be able to create tuples, access elements using indexing and slicing, and explain tuple immutability.

blocks.title: Building a tuple
blocks.content: A tuple is a collection of values kept in a fixed order. It looks a lot like a list, but it uses parentheses instead of square brackets, such as `("red", "green", "blue")`. You can store numbers, strings, or mixed data in one tuple. If a tuple has just one item, you need a trailing comma: `(5,)`. Without the comma, Python treats `(5)` as just the number `5` in parentheses, not a tuple.

blocks.title: Reading values with indexing and slicing
blocks.content: You access tuple values by position, the same way you do with lists. Index `0` gives the first item, index `1` gives the second, and negative indices count from the end, so `-1` gives the last item. Slicing lets you take a range of items, such as `days[1:4]`. The starting position is included, but the ending position is not. A slice returns a new tuple containing those values.

blocks.title: Tuples in action
blocks.content:
colors = ("red", "green", "blue", "yellow")

print(colors[0])
print(colors[-1])
print(colors[1:3])

single_value = (42,)
print(single_value)

blocks.title: When a tuple cannot change
blocks.content: Tuples are immutable, which means their contents cannot be changed after the tuple is created. You can read values from a tuple, but you cannot replace, remove, or add individual items inside it. For example, `colors[0] = "purple"` causes an error. This makes tuples useful when the group of values should stay the same.

blocks.title: Which line would fail?
blocks.content:
Consider this code:

`temps = (72, 68, 75, 70)`

Which expression returns `(68, 75)`, and which line would cause an error: `temps[1:3]` or `temps[1] = 69`?

→ `temps[1:3]` returns `(68, 75)`. `temps[1] = 69` causes an error because tuples are immutable and do not allow item assignment.

steps.stepGoal: Students will be able to compare tuples and lists by identifying their similarities and differences.

blocks.title: Two ways to store ordered data
blocks.content: Lists and tuples are both used to keep several values together in one variable. They are ordered, which means each item has a position, and they can hold different data types in the same collection. You can read items from either one with indexing, such as `[0]` for the first item, and both can be looped over. The big difference is whether the collection can change after it is created. A list is mutable, so you can add, remove, or replace items. A tuple is immutable, so its contents stay fixed.

blocks.title: How to recognize the difference
blocks.content:
The syntax gives you a quick clue about which one you are looking at. Lists use square brackets like `["tea", "coffee", "water"]`. Tuples usually use parentheses like `("tea", "coffee", "water")`. Their behavior is similar when you only need to read data, but different when you try to change it.

- List: can be changed after creation
- Tuple: cannot be changed after creation
- Both: keep order and support indexing

If you try to assign a new value into a tuple position, Python raises an error. That makes tuples useful when the values should stay the same.

blocks.title: Reading from both, changing only one
blocks.content:
colors_list = ["red", "green", "blue"]
colors_tuple = ("red", "green", "blue")

print(colors_list[1])   # green
print(colors_tuple[1])  # green

colors_list[1] = "yellow"
print(colors_list)      # ['red', 'yellow', 'blue']

# This would cause an error because tuples cannot be changed:
# colors_tuple[1] = "yellow"

blocks.title: Which line would fail?
blocks.content:
Look at this code:

items = ("pen", "pencil", "eraser")
items[0] = "marker"

What happens when Python reaches the second line?

→ It fails with an error because `items` is a tuple, and tuple elements cannot be reassigned.

blocks.title: Lab

blocks.title: Need a hint?
blocks.content: Both collections can be indexed the same way, but only one can be reassigned with something like `[1] = ...`. Leave the tuple as it is and make the change in the list.

steps.starterCode:
shopping_list = ["bread", "milk", "eggs"]
shopping_tuple = ("bread", "milk", "eggs")

# TODO: change the middle item in the list and print both collections
# Expected: the list shows a different second item, and the tuple stays the same
steps.expectedAction: Change the second value in the list, leave the tuple unchanged, and print both collections to show the difference.
steps.validationNote: Correct code should reassign the item at index 1 in `shopping_list` and then print both `shopping_list` and `shopping_tuple`, with only the list changed. A common mistake is trying to modify the tuple instead of using it as the unchanged comparison.

steps.stepGoal: Students will be able to work with lists inside tuples and tuples inside lists.

blocks.title: Structures can be nested
blocks.content:
A list or tuple can hold other collections as its items. That means you can have a tuple that contains lists, or a list that contains tuples. Python still uses positions to reach each level: first you choose the outer item, then the inner item.

For example, in `menu = (["eggs", "toast"], ["tea", "coffee"])`, `menu[0]` gives the first inner list, and `menu[0][1]` gives `"toast"`. The same pattern works when tuples are inside a list. The outer collection decides the first index, and the inner collection decides the second index.

blocks.title: Mutable inside immutable
blocks.content:
A tuple itself cannot be changed after it is created, but a list inside that tuple can still change. That surprises many beginners at first. The tuple keeps the same items in the same positions, but one of those items may be a list, and lists are mutable.

So this works: changing an element inside a list that lives in a tuple. What does not work is trying to replace the whole list with a different item by assigning into the tuple.

A good way to think about it is:

- tuple: fixed outer container
- list: changeable inner container

That distinction matters when you decide what kind of nested structure to build.

blocks.title: Reading and changing nested data
blocks.content:
trip = [
    ("Paris", 3),
    ("Rome", 2),
    ("Berlin", 4)
]

print(trip[1])        # ('Rome', 2)
print(trip[1][0])     # Rome
print(trip[2][1])     # 4

weekly_plan = (
    ["read", "walk"],
    ["code", "rest"]
)

weekly_plan[0][1] = "bike"
print(weekly_plan)    # (['read', 'bike'], ['code', 'rest'])

# This would fail because tuples do not allow item assignment:
# weekly_plan[0] = ["read", "bike"]

blocks.title: Which line would fail?
blocks.content:
Consider this code:

`groups = ([1, 2], [3, 4])`

Which line works, and which line causes an error?

`groups[1][0] = 9`
`groups[1] = [9, 4]`

→ `groups[1][0] = 9` works because it changes a value inside the inner list. `groups[1] = [9, 4]` causes an error because it tries to replace an item in the tuple itself.

steps.stepGoal: Students will be able to build dictionaries, access values by key, and add or remove key-value pairs.

blocks.title: Keys and values together
blocks.content: A dictionary stores information as key-value pairs. Each key acts like a label, and the value is the data connected to that label. Unlike a list, a dictionary is not about position, so you do not use index numbers like 0 or 1 to get values. You use the key instead, such as `book["title"]` or `profile["age"]`. This makes dictionaries a good fit when your data has named parts, like a person's name, a product's price, or a movie's year.

blocks.title: Reading, adding, and removing entries
blocks.content: You create a dictionary with curly braces: `{"name": "Maya", "score": 95}`. To read one value, put the key in square brackets after the dictionary name. You can also add a new pair by assigning a value to a new key, such as `student["grade"] = "A"`. If the key already exists, that assignment changes the old value. To remove a pair, use `pop()` with the key you want to remove. After that key is removed, it is no longer part of the dictionary.

blocks.title: A dictionary in action
blocks.content:
movie = {
    "title": "Inside Out",
    "year": 2015,
    "rating": "PG"
}

print(movie["title"])   # Inside Out

movie["genre"] = "Animation"
movie["year"] = 2016

movie.pop("rating")

print(movie)
# {'title': 'Inside Out', 'year': 2016, 'genre': 'Animation'}

blocks.title: Which line changes the dictionary?
blocks.content:
What does this code print?

```python
pet = {"type": "cat", "name": "Luna"}
pet["age"] = 3
pet.pop("type")
print(pet)
```

→ It prints `{'name': 'Luna', 'age': 3}`. The new key `"age"` is added, and `pop("type")` removes the `"type"` entry.

steps.stepGoal: Students will be able to iterate through dictionaries, including their keys and values.

blocks.title: Looping through a dictionary
blocks.content:
A dictionary can be used in a `for` loop, just like a list. When you loop over a dictionary directly, Python gives you the keys one at a time. That means `for key in scores:` is really a loop over the dictionary's keys.

This is useful when you want to use each key to look up its matching value. Inside the loop, `scores[key]` gets the value stored for that key. So a dictionary loop often works with two pieces of information: the key from the loop, and the value you fetch with that key.

blocks.title: Keys, values, and pairs
blocks.content:
Dictionaries have three common ways to iterate:

- `for key in data:` loops through keys.
- `for value in data.values():` loops through values.
- `for key, value in data.items():` loops through key-value pairs.

These are similar, but they do different jobs. Use keys when the key names matter, values when you only care about the stored data, and `items()` when you want both together. `items()` is often the clearest choice when you plan to print or process each key with its matching value.

blocks.title: Three ways to iterate
Which loop gives both pieces?
blocks.content:
If `book = {"title": "Dune", "pages": 412}`, which loop lets you print `title : Dune` and `pages : 412` without doing another lookup?

→ `for key, value in book.items():` does that, because `items()` gives each key together with its matching value. Looping over `book` alone only gives the keys.

blocks.title: Need a hint?
blocks.content: One loop should give you both the player name and the score together. A second loop should go through just the values in the dictionary.

steps.starterCode:

# TODO: print each player with their score, then print only the score values
# Expected: three lines with player-score pairs, followed by three lines showing only the scores

steps.validationNote: Correct code should print three player-score pair lines and then three lines containing only the numeric scores from the same dictionary. A common mistake is looping over the dictionary directly both times, which prints keys instead of values in the second part.

steps.stepGoal: Students will be able to check whether specific keys exist in a dictionary.

blocks.title: Checking whether a key is present
blocks.content: A dictionary does not guarantee that every key you want is already there, so it helps to check before you use one. In Python, the simplest way to do that is with the `in` keyword. When you write `'email' in profile`, Python checks the dictionary's keys and gives you `True` if that key exists and `False` if it does not. This is different from checking values: `in` on a dictionary looks at keys by default, not the stored values. That makes it a clean way to ask, "Does this dictionary have this key?"

blocks.title: Using `in` with a dictionary
blocks.content:
student = {
    "name": "Maya",
    "grade": "A",
    "city": "Denver"
}

print("name" in student)      # True
print("email" in student)     # False
print("Maya" in student)      # False, because Python checks keys here

blocks.title: Keys or values?
blocks.content:
What does this print?

info = {"animal": "cat", "color": "black"}
print("black" in info)

→ It prints `False`. The `in` keyword checks whether `"black"` is a key in the dictionary, and here it is a value, not a key.

blocks.title: Need a hint?
blocks.content: Use the key as a string and test it against the dictionary itself. The result of that expression can be printed directly.

steps.starterCode:
account = {

    "plan": "basic",
    "active": True
}

# TODO: Check whether the key "email" exists in the account dictionary and print the result

steps.validationNote: Correct code should print `False` because `account` does not contain the key `"email"`. A common mistake is checking for a value instead of a key, or using the key name without quotes.

steps.stepGoal: Students will be able to use the keys(), items(), and values() methods to inspect dictionary contents.

blocks.title: Inspecting a dictionary
blocks.content:
A dictionary can hold many key-value pairs, so it helps to have a quick way to look at just the keys, just the values, or both together. Python gives you methods for that: `keys()`, `values()`, and `items()`. These methods do not pull out one specific entry by name. Instead, they let you inspect the dictionary as a whole.

Think of them like three different views of the same data:

- `keys()` shows only the dictionary's keys.
- `values()` shows only the dictionary's values.
- `items()` shows each key paired with its value.

That makes them useful when you want to see what information a dictionary contains or print it in a readable way.

blocks.title: Keys, values, and pairs in action
blocks.content:
book = {
    "title": "The Hobbit",
    "author": "J.R.R. Tolkien",
    "pages": 310
}

print(book.keys())
print(book.values())
print(book.items())

blocks.title: What each method returns
blocks.content:
`keys()`, `values()`, and `items()` each return a special view of the dictionary's contents. For a beginner, the important part is what you can see when you print them. `keys()` prints the key names, `values()` prints the stored data, and `items()` prints pairs that look like tuples, such as `('title', 'The Hobbit')`.

`items()` is especially helpful because it keeps each key connected to its value. If you only print `keys()` or only print `values()`, you lose that pairing. So if you want to inspect complete entries, `items()` is usually the clearest choice.

blocks.title: Which method matches the goal?
blocks.content:
A dictionary named `movie` stores `"title"`, `"year"`, and `"rating"`. Which method should you use if you want to see each key together with its value?

→ Use `movie.items()`. It returns key-value pairs, so each piece of information stays matched with its label.

blocks.title: Lab
blocks.content: A small dictionary of weather data is waiting in the editor. Print three views of it: the keys, the values, and the full key-value pairs. A correct result will show all three, with the pairs appearing together in the final output.

blocks.title: Not sure which method fits?
blocks.content: If the output should show `city` next to `Lisbon` as one pair, you need the method that returns both parts together, not just one list of labels or one list of data.

steps.starterCode:
weather = {
    "city": "Lisbon",
    "temperature": 72,
    "condition": "Sunny"
}

# TODO: print the dictionary's keys, values, and key-value pairs
# Expected: three printouts showing the labels, the stored data, and the complete pairs
steps.expectedAction: Print the weather dictionary using its keys view, its values view, and its items view.
steps.validationNote: Correct code should print three lines based on `weather.keys()`, `weather.values()`, and `weather.items()`. A common mistake is printing the whole dictionary or using only one of the methods instead of all three.
